accepted_variants: A frame in which Newton's first law holds.
cards.definition: An inertial frame is a reference frame in which a free particle moves with constant velocity. Frames moving at constant velocity relative to an inertial frame are also inertial in Newtonian mechanics.
major_error_concepts: Calling every stationary-looking laboratory frame exactly inertial regardless of acceleration.
cards.prompt: What is Inertial Frame? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Force-free motion has constant velocity.
Constant-velocity translations preserve inertial character.

accepted_variants: The vector r specifying location relative to an origin.
cards.definition: A position vector points from a chosen origin to a particle's location. Its components depend on the coordinate system and can vary with time.
major_error_concepts: Treating position as independent of the chosen origin.
cards.prompt: What is Position Vector? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Vector from chosen origin to particle.
Coordinates depend on the reference choice.

cards.definition: Displacement is the change in position vector, delta r = r_final - r_initial. It depends only on the endpoints and differs from the scalar distance traveled along a path.
major_error_concepts: Identifying displacement magnitude with total distance for every trajectory.
cards.prompt: What is Displacement? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Final minus initial position.
Displacement is a vector and need not equal path length.

accepted_variants: Instantaneous vector rate of change of location.
cards.definition: Instantaneous velocity is the time derivative of position, v = dr/dt. It points tangent to the trajectory, and its magnitude is speed.
major_error_concepts: Treating speed and velocity as identical vector quantities.
cards.prompt: What is Velocity? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Time derivative of position.
Speed is the magnitude of velocity.

accepted_variants: Instantaneous vector rate of velocity change.
cards.definition: Acceleration is the time derivative of velocity, a = dv/dt. It can arise from a change in speed, direction, or both; constant speed does not imply zero acceleration.
major_error_concepts: Claiming uniform circular motion has zero acceleration because speed is constant.
cards.prompt: What is Acceleration? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Derivative of velocity.
Directional change also produces acceleration.

accepted_variants: The proportionality between net force and acceleration.
cards.definition: Inertial mass measures a body's resistance to acceleration under a given net force. In Newtonian mechanics with constant mass, a = F_net/m; mass is a scalar property distinct from weight.
major_error_concepts: Measuring mass in newtons or treating it as location-dependent weight.
cards.prompt: What is Inertial Mass? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Mass sets response to net force.
Mass differs from gravitational force or weight.

cards.definition: The particle approximation treats a body's mass as concentrated at one point when its size, shape, and rotation are irrelevant to the question. It does not claim the real body is physically dimensionless.
major_error_concepts: Using a point-particle model to determine an extended body's rotational inertia.
cards.prompt: What is Particle Approximation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Ignore size and orientation when they do not affect the modeled motion.
Approximation depends on the question and scale.

accepted_variants: The location R defined by the first spatial mass moment divided by total mass.
cards.definition: The center of mass is the mass-weighted mean position: R = sum(m_i r_i)/M, with an integral for continuous matter. It can lie outside the material of the object.
major_error_concepts: Taking an unweighted position average when masses differ.
cards.prompt: What is Center of Mass? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Mass-weighted average position.
Need not coincide with a material point or geometric center.

accepted_variants: Forces exchanged among members of the system.
cards.definition: Internal forces are interactions between constituents that both belong to the chosen system. Their classification depends on the system boundary; under Newtonian action-reaction assumptions their vector sum cancels in the system's linear-momentum balance.
major_error_concepts: Calling a force internal solely because it acts inside the geometric outline of one body.
cards.prompt: What is Internal Forces? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Both interacting bodies are inside the chosen system.
System choice determines whether a force is internal.

accepted_variants: Forces applied by the environment to the selected system.
cards.definition: External forces are forces exerted on a system by objects outside its chosen boundary. Their vector sum controls the total linear momentum change of that system under ordinary Newtonian assumptions.
major_error_concepts: Including both sides of an internal action-reaction pair in the external force total.
cards.prompt: What is External Forces? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Source lies outside the chosen system.
Classification changes when the system boundary changes.

cards.definition: Net force is the vector sum of all forces acting on the selected body or system. Component signs and directions matter; a nonzero collection of forces can have zero resultant.
major_error_concepts: Adding force magnitudes without their directions.
cards.prompt: What is Net Force? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Vector sum of forces.
Nonzero individual forces may cancel.

accepted_variants: Weight is the local gravitational force.
cards.definition: Near Earth's surface, the gravitational force on a mass is approximately m g directed downward, with g treated as locally constant. Weight in this usage means gravitational force and is distinct from a scale's normal-force reading.
major_error_concepts: Saying gravitational force vanishes whenever a falling object is weightless on a scale.
cards.prompt: What is Weight? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Near-surface gravitational force is m g downward.
Distinguish gravity from apparent weight or support force.

cards.definition: A normal force is the contact force component perpendicular to a contacting surface. Its magnitude is determined by the constraints and dynamics, and need not equal the body's weight.
major_error_concepts: Assuming normal force equals weight on every incline or accelerating surface.
cards.prompt: What is Normal Force? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Perpendicular contact-force component.
Magnitude follows from the situation, not an automatic equality to m g.

accepted_variants: Axial pulling force carried by a taut connector.
cards.definition: Tension is a pulling force transmitted along a taut string, cable, or similar connector. An ideal massless string over ideal pulleys is modeled with uniform tension along a continuous segment; real connectors can violate that simplification.
major_error_concepts: Making a flexible ideal string push on an attached body.
cards.prompt: What is Tension? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Pulling force along the connector.
Uniform tension requires appropriate idealizations.

cards.definition: Static friction is the tangential contact force that prevents impending relative sliding. Its magnitude adjusts as needed up to a bound, usually modeled as |f_s| <= mu_s N, rather than always equaling that maximum.
major_error_concepts: Setting static friction equal to mu_s N in every resting configuration.
cards.prompt: What is Static Friction? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Opposes impending relative slip.
Magnitude is bounded, not always at the bound.

cards.definition: Kinetic friction acts along a sliding contact and opposes relative sliding of the surfaces. A common dry-friction approximation is f_k = mu_k N; the coefficient and adequacy of the model depend on the materials and conditions.
major_error_concepts: Assuming friction must oppose the center-of-mass velocity in every reference frame.
cards.prompt: What is Kinetic Friction? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Opposes relative sliding at the contact.
mu_k N is an approximate magnitude model.

cards.definition: In the Hooke-law regime, a spring exerts F = -k x along its deformation coordinate, where x is measured from equilibrium. The negative sign indicates a restoring direction; the linear law is valid only over a limited deformation range.
major_error_concepts: Using total spring length rather than extension from equilibrium as x.
cards.prompt: What is Hooke's Law? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Force proportional to displacement from equilibrium.
Restoring sign and limited linear regime.

cards.definition: Drag is a resistive force associated with motion relative to a surrounding medium. Models such as F = -b v or F = -c |v|v apply in different flow regimes, with v taken relative to the medium.
major_error_concepts: Using one universal drag formula for every speed, shape, and fluid.
cards.prompt: What is Drag Force? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Resistance depends on relative motion through the medium.
Linear and quadratic speed models have different applicability.

cards.definition: Linear momentum of a Newtonian particle is p = m v. It is a vector and the momentum of a system is the vector sum of its constituents' momenta.
major_error_concepts: Equating momentum with the scalar kinetic energy.
cards.prompt: What is Linear Momentum? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: p equals mass times velocity.
System momentum is a vector sum.

accepted_variants: Area under a force-time curve, component by component.
cards.definition: Impulse is the time integral of a force: J = integral F dt. It is a vector with units of momentum; for constant force it equals F delta t.
major_error_concepts: Integrating force over displacement to obtain impulse.
cards.prompt: What is Impulse? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Time integral of force.
Direction and sign matter.

cards.definition: Translational equilibrium means zero net external force, so the center of mass has zero acceleration. It may be at rest or moving with constant velocity.
major_error_concepts: Concluding that zero net force requires the object to be stationary.
cards.prompt: What is Translational Equilibrium? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Net external force is zero.
Equilibrium does not require zero velocity.

accepted_variants: Force component along motion times displacement.
cards.definition: Work by a constant force over displacement delta r is W = F dot delta r = F delta r cos theta. It measures energy transfer along the displacement and may be positive, negative, or zero.
major_error_concepts: Using force magnitude times path length when the force is perpendicular to motion.
cards.prompt: What is Work by a Constant Force? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Dot product of force and displacement.
Only the displacement-parallel force component contributes.

cards.definition: Work by a spatially varying force along a path is W = integral F dot dr. The integral follows the actual path; in one dimension it is the signed area under the force-position curve.
major_error_concepts: Replacing the line integral by endpoint force times displacement without justification.
cards.prompt: What is Work by a Variable Force? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Line integral along the path.
May depend on the path for nonconservative forces.

accepted_variants: Energy associated with particle motion in a specified frame.
cards.definition: The translational kinetic energy of a Newtonian particle is K = one-half m v squared. It is nonnegative and depends on the reference frame through speed.
major_error_concepts: Assigning negative kinetic energy merely because velocity is negative.
cards.prompt: What is Kinetic Energy? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: K = m v squared divided by two.
Scalar and frame-dependent.

accepted_variants: Energy function whose negative gradient generates the conservative force.
cards.definition: A conservative force admits a potential energy U such that its work equals -delta U. Equivalently F = -gradient U where the potential is differentiable; the additive zero of U is arbitrary.
major_error_concepts: Using F = positive gradient U.
Assuming potential energy must always be nonnegative.
cards.prompt: What is Potential Energy? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Conservative work equals negative potential-energy change.
Only potential differences matter to the force.

cards.definition: Mechanical energy is the sum of kinetic and potential energies, E_mech = K + U, for the modeled system. It need not remain constant when nonconservative interactions transfer energy into other forms.
major_error_concepts: Claiming mechanical energy is conserved in every frictional process.
cards.prompt: What is Mechanical Energy? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Sum K + U.
Distinguish mechanical-energy conservation from total-energy conservation.

cards.definition: Power is the rate of energy transfer or work, P = dW/dt. For a force acting on a particle with velocity v, instantaneous mechanical power is F dot v.
major_error_concepts: Confusing power with total work or energy.
cards.prompt: What is Power? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Energy transfer per unit time.
Force power is F dot v.

cards.definition: Newton's universal gravitational force between point masses is attractive, has magnitude G m1 m2/r squared, and acts along the line joining them. The same exterior result applies to spherically symmetric masses treated from outside.
major_error_concepts: Applying the exterior point-mass formula inside every extended mass distribution without modification.
cards.prompt: What is Universal Gravitation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Inverse-square attractive force proportional to both masses.
Separation is between point masses or spherical centers in the appropriate case.

cards.definition: Gravitational field g at a point is gravitational force per unit test mass: g = F_grav/m. For a point source M it points toward the source with magnitude G M/r squared.
major_error_concepts: Including the test mass as a multiplicative factor in g.
cards.prompt: What is Gravitational Field? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Force per unit test mass.
Direction toward a positive gravitating point source.

cards.definition: For constant acceleration, v = v0 + a t and r = r0 + v0 t + one-half a t squared. The equations apply componentwise; the scalar relation v squared = v0 squared + 2 a delta x applies to one-dimensional constant-acceleration motion.
major_error_concepts: Applying the formulas unchanged to time-varying acceleration.
cards.prompt: What is Constant-Acceleration Kinematics? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Acceleration must remain constant.
Vector relations can be resolved into components.

accepted_variants: Independent component equations coupled by one flight time.
cards.definition: Ideal projectile motion under uniform gravity has constant horizontal velocity and vertical acceleration -g when drag is neglected and axes are chosen horizontally and upward. The components share the same elapsed time even though their accelerations differ.
major_error_concepts: Assuming horizontal velocity vanishes at the top of the trajectory.
cards.prompt: What is Projectile Motion? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Horizontal acceleration zero and vertical acceleration -g.
Common time parameter and neglected drag.

cards.definition: Newton's first law states that in an inertial frame a body with zero net force remains at rest or moves with constant velocity. Sustaining constant velocity does not require a continuing nonzero resultant force.
major_error_concepts: Claiming a moving body requires net force in its direction of travel to keep moving.
cards.prompt: What is Newton's First Law? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Zero net force gives constant velocity in an inertial frame.

accepted_variants: The vector equation of translational dynamics.
cards.definition: Newton's second law relates net external force to momentum change: F_net = dp/dt in an inertial frame. For a constant-mass particle this becomes F_net = m a.
major_error_concepts: Equating one arbitrarily chosen force with m a when other forces also act.
cards.prompt: What is Newton's Second Law? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Net force changes momentum.
F = m a assumes constant mass and an inertial frame.

cards.definition: Newton's third law states that two interacting bodies exert equal-magnitude opposite-direction forces on each other in the elementary Newtonian setting. The pair acts on different bodies, so it does not cancel in a single body's force balance.
major_error_concepts: Pairing a body's weight and its normal force as a third-law pair.
cards.prompt: What is Newton's Third Law? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Equal and opposite interaction forces.
They act on different bodies.

accepted_variants: The resultant is the sum of individual forces.
cards.definition: Force superposition means the net force is obtained by vector addition of all applicable interaction forces. Each contribution is resolved in a common coordinate system before combining components.
major_error_concepts: Adding unsigned magnitudes for forces with different directions.
cards.prompt: What is Force Superposition? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Vector addition of force contributions.
Use a common coordinate system.

accepted_variants: Third-law pairs cannot be cancelled on one body's diagram.
cards.definition: An action-reaction pair has one force on each of two interacting bodies. Both cancel when summing internal forces for the combined system, but only one belongs on each body's individual free-body diagram.
major_error_concepts: Removing an applied force from a single-body diagram because its reaction exists elsewhere.
cards.prompt: What is Action–Reaction Pair Boundaries? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: One force on each body.
Cancellation depends on choosing the combined system.

accepted_variants: The integrated kinetic-energy form of Newton's second law.
cards.definition: The work-energy theorem states that net work on a constant-mass particle equals its kinetic-energy change: W_net = delta K. It includes work by both conservative and nonconservative forces.
major_error_concepts: Equating net work with total mechanical-energy change in every situation.
cards.prompt: What is Work–Energy Theorem? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Net work equals kinetic-energy change.
All force contributions to work are included.

accepted_variants: Delta K + delta U = 0 for the conservative system.
cards.definition: Mechanical energy K + U is conserved when all working interactions in the model are conservative and no unaccounted energy transfer crosses the system boundary. Kinetic and potential energy can change individually while their sum remains fixed.
major_error_concepts: Imposing mechanical-energy conservation across a dissipative collision without accounting for internal energy.
cards.prompt: What is Mechanical-Energy Conservation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Conservative interactions and appropriate system boundary.
Conserved sum does not require K and U individually constant.

accepted_variants: Energy bookkeeping including nonconservative work and thermal effects.
cards.definition: When nonconservative forces do work, changes in K + U must be balanced against transfers to other energy forms or across the system boundary. Friction may convert mechanical energy to internal energy without violating total-energy conservation.
major_error_concepts: Claiming friction violates conservation of energy.
cards.prompt: What is Nonconservative Energy Accounting? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Mechanical-energy loss is not destruction of total energy.
Track boundary transfers and internal-energy changes consistently.

accepted_variants: The time-integrated form of the momentum equation.
cards.definition: The impulse-momentum theorem states that net impulse equals the change in total linear momentum: integral F_net dt = delta p. It remains useful when the detailed time dependence of a brief force is unknown.
major_error_concepts: Using a single contact impulse as the net impulse when other appreciable impulses act.
cards.prompt: What is Impulse–Momentum Theorem? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Net impulse equals momentum change.
Vector relationship.

accepted_variants: Since dP/dt = F_external,net, P is constant when the external resultant vanishes at every time; equal and opposite impulses at different times only restore the original P afterward.
cards.definition: For a fixed Newtonian system in an inertial frame, total linear momentum remains constant throughout an interval if the net external force is zero throughout that interval. More generally, the momentum change equals external impulse. Zero impulse over one selected interval guarantees equal initial and final momenta, not constancy at every intermediate time. Internal interactions may redistribute momentum among constituents.
major_error_concepts: Claiming that canceling external impulses at different times imply momentum never changed in between.
Concluding each constituent's momentum is separately conserved during an isolated collision.
cards.prompt: What is Momentum Conservation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Zero net external force throughout the interval keeps total momentum constant for a fixed system in an inertial frame.
Zero net impulse over only the whole interval guarantees endpoint equality; individual constituents may still change momentum.

accepted_variants: Reasoning with dimensions such as mass, length, and time.
cards.definition: Dimensional analysis checks whether quantities combined or equated have compatible physical dimensions. It can constrain a relation's form or identify dimensionless groups, but cannot generally determine pure numerical coefficients or prove the physics correct.
major_error_concepts: Treating a dimensionally correct equation as automatically physically true.
cards.prompt: What is Dimensional Analysis? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Dimensionally compatible terms and equations.
Dimensional consistency is necessary but not sufficient.

cards.definition: A scaling argument estimates how an outcome changes when controlling quantities change by comparing powers, dominant terms, or dimensionless ratios. The conclusion depends on maintaining the assumed physical regime and which quantities are held fixed.
major_error_concepts: Extending one regime's power-law scaling across a change in dominant forces.
cards.prompt: What is Scaling Arguments? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Track proportional changes within stated assumptions.
Dominant balance can change between regimes.

cards.definition: A physical quantity is a measurable or model-defined property represented by a magnitude together with units when dimensional. Its meaning includes what is measured and the conditions under which it is defined.
major_error_concepts: Reporting a dimensional measurement as a bare number with no unit or context.
cards.prompt: What is Physical Quantity? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Magnitude with a physical interpretation and appropriate unit.

accepted_variants: Fundamental reference units and their algebraic combinations.
cards.definition: Base units are selected independent reference units; derived units are combinations used for other quantities. For example, speed uses length per time and force uses mass times length per time squared.
major_error_concepts: Treating a new named derived unit as a new independent physical dimension automatically.
cards.prompt: What is Base and Derived Units? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Derived units combine base units.
A chosen basis does not make derived quantities less physical.

cards.definition: An SI prefix multiplies a unit by a defined power of ten, such as kilo for 10^3 or milli for 10^-3. The prefix is part of the unit and is raised to powers with it when units are squared or cubed.
major_error_concepts: Converting one square centimeter to 10^-2 square meters instead of 10^-4.
cards.prompt: What is SI Prefix? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Power-of-ten unit multiplier.
Area and volume require applying the power to the prefix too.

cards.definition: A physical dimension identifies a quantity's type, such as length, mass, or time, independently of the particular unit chosen. Meters and feet represent the same dimension but different units.
major_error_concepts: Treating meters and centimeters as different dimensions.
cards.prompt: What is Physical Dimension? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Quantity type independent of unit scale.

accepted_variants: Dimensional conversion through cancelling unit factors.
cards.definition: Unit conversion multiplies by ratios of equivalent quantities equal to one, so units cancel while the physical quantity stays unchanged. Conversion factors must be oriented and powered consistently.
major_error_concepts: Changing the unit label without changing the numerical value when scales differ.
cards.prompt: What is Unit Conversion? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Multiply by equivalence ratios.
Physical amount unchanged while numerical representation changes.

cards.definition: An order-of-magnitude estimate describes a quantity's scale using powers of ten rather than exact digits. Rounding conventions vary, so the intended precision of the comparison should be clear.
major_error_concepts: Treating an order-of-magnitude estimate as an exact significant-digit calculation.
cards.prompt: What is Order of Magnitude? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Approximate power-of-ten scale.

cards.definition: Scientific notation writes a nonzero number as a times 10^n with integer n and coefficient magnitude between one and ten. It makes scale and significant digits easier to distinguish.
major_error_concepts: Dropping the exponent when comparing numerical scales.
cards.prompt: What is Scientific Notation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Normalized coefficient times integer power of ten.

accepted_variants: Meaningful reported digits under a stated convention.
cards.definition: Significant figures communicate a numerical reporting precision compatible with a measurement or calculation. They do not replace an explicit uncertainty model and do not by themselves establish accuracy.
major_error_concepts: Assuming more printed digits prove a more accurate measurement.
cards.prompt: What is Significant Figures? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Reporting precision rather than complete error analysis.

accepted_variants: The estimated uncertainty attached to a measurement.
cards.definition: Measurement uncertainty quantifies the range or distribution of values reasonably associated with a measured quantity under a stated model. It reflects limited information rather than a known signed mistake.
major_error_concepts: Treating uncertainty as the exact difference from an unknown true value.
cards.prompt: What is Measurement Uncertainty? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Quantified limitation on knowledge of the measured value.
Interpretation depends on the uncertainty model.

accepted_variants: Closeness of repeated results to one another.
cards.definition: Precision describes agreement among repeated measurements or the narrowness of their scatter under stated conditions. A precise set can still be systematically displaced from the reference value.
major_error_concepts: Inferring absence of bias from tightly clustered measurements.
cards.prompt: What is Measurement Precision? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Repeatability or low scatter.
Not identical to accuracy.

cards.definition: Accuracy describes closeness to a reference or true value in the relevant context. It depends on both systematic and random effects and is not established merely by fine instrument resolution.
major_error_concepts: Calling a consistently biased instrument accurate because it displays many digits.
cards.prompt: What is Measurement Accuracy? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Closeness to the relevant reference value.
Different from precision or resolution.

cards.definition: Random error is variation that changes unpredictably across observations under the measurement model. Repetition can help estimate and reduce uncertainty in an average when independence and other assumptions hold.
major_error_concepts: Assuming averaging always removes correlated or systematic effects.
cards.prompt: What is Random Error? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Observation-to-observation random variation.
Averaging benefits require assumptions.

cards.definition: A systematic error is a repeatable or structured deviation associated with calibration, method, or conditions. Repeating the same biased procedure does not generally remove it.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a large sample automatically eliminates a miscalibrated scale's offset.
cards.prompt: What is Systematic Error? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Structured bias or repeatable deviation.
Repetition alone does not correct it.

cards.definition: Instrument resolution is the smallest change distinguishable by the instrument's readout or response under specified conditions. It is only one contributor to overall measurement uncertainty.
major_error_concepts: Using display resolution as proof of total measurement accuracy.
cards.prompt: What is Instrument Resolution? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Smallest distinguishable increment.
Resolution is not complete uncertainty or accuracy.

accepted_variants: A reported measurement range with a stated confidence or coverage convention.
cards.definition: An uncertainty interval reports a range around an estimate with a stated interpretation, such as a coverage interval under a measurement model. Its endpoints are not automatically guaranteed absolute bounds on every possible value.
major_error_concepts: Treating any plus-or-minus range as a guaranteed bound without knowing its definition.
cards.prompt: What is Uncertainty Interval? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Range with an explicit coverage or uncertainty meaning.

accepted_variants: Percentage deviation from a comparison value.
cards.definition: Percent error compares a measurement with a nonzero reference using 100 times the difference divided by the reference magnitude, with signed or absolute convention specified. It differs from uncertainty when the reference is not known exactly.
major_error_concepts: Calling percent error the same as relative uncertainty in every experiment.
cards.prompt: What is Percent Error? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Reference-based relative difference times 100 percent.
State sign convention and nonzero reference.

cards.definition: Relative uncertainty is an uncertainty measure divided by the magnitude of the measured estimate. It is dimensionless and can be expressed as a percentage, but is ill-conditioned when the estimate is near zero.
major_error_concepts: Interpreting a huge fractional uncertainty near zero without considering the absolute scale.
cards.prompt: What is Relative Uncertainty? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Uncertainty relative to the value's magnitude.
Near-zero denominator is problematic.

accepted_variants: Propagation of input uncertainty through a formula.
cards.definition: First-order uncertainty propagation combines input uncertainties according to a derived quantity's sensitivity to them. Independent standard uncertainties commonly combine in quadrature after derivative weighting; correlations require covariance terms.
major_error_concepts: Adding all input percentages regardless of the functional relationship and dependence.
cards.prompt: What is Uncertainty Propagation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Sensitivity-weighted combination.
Correlated inputs need covariance contributions.

accepted_variants: Rate represented by a plotted slope.
cards.definition: A graph's secant slope is the change in vertical quantity divided by change in horizontal quantity. Its units are vertical-axis units per horizontal-axis unit, and its physical interpretation depends on what is plotted.
major_error_concepts: Interpreting every graph slope as speed regardless of the plotted quantities.
cards.prompt: What is Graph Slope? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Rise over run with corresponding units.
Meaning depends on axes.

accepted_variants: Integral-like accumulated quantity from a graph.
cards.definition: Signed area under a quantity-versus-variable graph accumulates the product of those quantities over the horizontal interval. For example, velocity-time area gives displacement, while force-position area gives work when the force component is appropriate.
major_error_concepts: Calling every area under any graph displacement.
cards.prompt: What is Area under a Graph? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Accumulation with product units and sign.
Interpretation depends on axis variables.

accepted_variants: Straight-line representation of a specified nonlinear model.
cards.definition: A linearized plot transforms variables so a proposed nonlinear relation becomes a straight-line model, such as plotting y against x squared for y=a x squared. The transformation changes error behavior and does not prove the model merely by making a line look plausible.
major_error_concepts: Assuming visual straightness alone establishes causation or exact model validity.
cards.prompt: What is Linearized Plot? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Transform coordinates to expose a proposed linear relation.
Measurement-error interpretation changes with transformation.

cards.definition: A power-law model has form y=A x^n over a specified domain and regime. On positive data, logarithms turn it into log y=log A+n log x, so the exponent becomes a log-log slope.
major_error_concepts: Applying logarithms to nonpositive values without redefining the model or domain.
cards.prompt: What is Power-Law Model? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Power dependence with stated regime.
Log-log slope is exponent for positive quantities.

cards.definition: A scalar is a quantity described by one value that does not transform as a spatial direction vector. It may be positive, negative, or zero depending on the quantity and convention.
major_error_concepts: Calling every negative quantity a vector because sign implies a direction.
cards.prompt: What is Scalar? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: No vector direction.
Scalar does not mean always positive.

accepted_variants: The projections or basis coordinates describing a vector.
cards.definition: Vector components are the signed coefficients of a vector along chosen coordinate basis directions. Components change when the basis changes even when the geometric vector is unchanged.
major_error_concepts: Treating one component as the full vector magnitude in all orientations.
cards.prompt: What is Vector Components? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Signed coordinate coefficients.
Basis-dependent representation.

cards.definition: A unit vector has magnitude one and specifies a direction. Multiplying it by a signed scalar gives a vector along that direction with the corresponding magnitude and orientation.
major_error_concepts: Assuming unit vector means a vector measured in one particular physical unit.
cards.prompt: What is Unit Vector? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Magnitude one with directional role.

cards.definition: Vector addition combines components in a common basis or uses the head-to-tail geometric rule. The magnitude of a sum generally differs from the sum of magnitudes.
major_error_concepts: Adding lengths without accounting for directions.
cards.prompt: What is Vector Addition? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Add corresponding components in one basis.
Magnitude is not generally additive.

accepted_variants: Inner or scalar product in Euclidean coordinates.
cards.definition: The dot product u dot v equals the sum of corresponding component products and equals |u||v|cos theta. It yields a scalar and selects the parallel contribution used in quantities such as work.
major_error_concepts: Using sine rather than cosine for the dot-product angle relation.
cards.prompt: What is Dot Product? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Scalar product with cosine-angle dependence.

cards.definition: The three-dimensional cross product has magnitude |u||v|sin theta and direction perpendicular to both vectors by the right-hand rule. Reversing the operand order reverses its sign.
major_error_concepts: Treating u cross v as equal to v cross u.
cards.prompt: What is Cross Product? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Perpendicular vector with sine magnitude.
Order matters.

cards.definition: A coordinate system assigns numbers to locations using a chosen origin and axes or other coordinate rules. Changing coordinates changes numerical descriptions without necessarily changing the physical situation.
major_error_concepts: Confusing a coordinate relabeling with a physical motion of the object.
cards.prompt: What is Coordinate System? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Chosen origin and coordinate convention describe positions.

accepted_variants: The physical observational framework for coordinates and time.
cards.definition: A reference frame supplies the observer-related spatial and temporal description used to state motion. Relative velocity and acceleration must be interpreted in that frame; inertial character is an additional physical property.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every coordinate system automatically represents an inertial frame.
cards.prompt: What is Reference Frame? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Observer-based description of events and motion.
Frame choice and inertial status differ.

accepted_variants: A tractable representation of a physical system.
cards.definition: A physical model is a simplified representation connecting assumptions, variables, and relationships to predictions. Its value depends on the questions and regimes it captures, not on reproducing every detail of reality.
major_error_concepts: Rejecting every idealized model merely because it omits some real-world detail.
cards.prompt: What is Physical Model? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Simplified assumption-based representation.
Scope tied to intended predictions.

cards.definition: A model assumption is a condition adopted to define or simplify a calculation, such as negligible drag or constant mass. Its consequences and domain of adequacy should be explicit rather than hidden in the algebra.
major_error_concepts: Treating an approximation assumption as a universally exact physical law.
cards.prompt: What is Model Assumption? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Condition shaping the model.
Validity depends on the use case.

accepted_variants: Domain of adequacy for an approximation.
cards.definition: An approximation regime is the range of scales or conditions where neglected effects are small enough for the intended accuracy. Leaving that regime can require a different model even if the original algebra remains consistent.
major_error_concepts: Applying one approximation unchanged after its neglected term becomes dominant.
cards.prompt: What is Approximation Regime? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Conditions make omitted effects acceptably small.
Accuracy target matters.

accepted_variants: An expected observable derived from a model.
cards.definition: A prediction is a consequence of a specified model and input assumptions that can be compared with observations. Agreement supports adequacy for that comparison but does not uniquely establish every assumption.
major_error_concepts: Treating one matching result as proof that no other model could explain it.
cards.prompt: What is Prediction? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Model consequence testable against observations.
Agreement does not prove model uniqueness.

cards.definition: A testable hypothesis makes claims connected to possible observations that could count against it under stated conditions. A failed comparison must consider auxiliary assumptions and measurement limitations as well as the focal claim.
major_error_concepts: Calling a claim empirically tested when every conceivable outcome is declared supporting.
cards.prompt: What is Testable Hypothesis? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Observable implications permit meaningful challenge.
Testing involves measurement and auxiliary assumptions.

accepted_variants: A comparison designed to isolate a factor.
cards.definition: A controlled comparison isolates a proposed influence by comparing conditions while accounting for other relevant differences. Controls improve causal interpretation but do not automatically remove every confounder.
major_error_concepts: Assuming any two groups form a controlled experiment regardless of their differences.
cards.prompt: What is Controlled Comparison? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Compare conditions while managing alternative explanations.

accepted_variants: Distinguishing statistical co-variation from causal effect.
cards.definition: Correlation is an observed association between quantities; causation asserts that changing one can produce change in another under a defined causal setting. Shared causes, selection, or chance can produce correlation without the proposed direct cause.
major_error_concepts: Inferring a direct causal mechanism solely from a correlated plot.
cards.prompt: What is Correlation and Causation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Association differs from causal influence.
Alternative explanations can generate association.

cards.definition: A system boundary specifies which objects or material belong to the system and which interactions cross into the surroundings. Internal and external force or energy classifications depend on that choice.
major_error_concepts: Changing a system boundary while keeping all force and energy terms classified as before.
cards.prompt: What is System Boundary? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Defines included components.
Determines internal versus external transfers.

cards.definition: An interaction diagram identifies the objects and the physical interactions among them before equations are written. It helps separate contact and long-range interactions and supports consistent force accounting.
major_error_concepts: Drawing velocity as an interaction force between objects.
cards.prompt: What is Interaction Diagram? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Map objects and their interactions.

cards.definition: A free-body diagram shows forces acting on one selected object or system, with each force attributed to an interaction. It omits the reaction forces acting on other bodies and does not add velocity or acceleration as extra forces.
major_error_concepts: Adding an independent force of motion in the direction of velocity.
cards.prompt: What is Free-Body Diagram? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Forces on the selected body only.
Do not include third-law partners acting elsewhere.

cards.definition: For a small angle theta measured in radians, sin theta is approximately theta and cos theta approximately 1-theta squared/2. The errors grow with angle, so small must be judged relative to the required accuracy.
major_error_concepts: Substituting degree-valued numbers directly into sin theta approximately theta.
cards.prompt: What is Small-Angle Approximation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Radian-based approximations.
Accuracy depends on angle size.

cards.definition: Density is mass per unit volume, rho=m/V for a homogeneous sample or an average over the specified region. Local density can vary spatially, and its value depends on material state and conditions.
major_error_concepts: Treating equal density as proof that two samples are the same substance.
cards.prompt: What is Density? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Mass divided by volume.
Local or average interpretation must be specified.

accepted_variants: Normal stress or force intensity on a surface.
cards.definition: Pressure is normal force per unit area in the appropriate local or averaged description. Its SI unit is the pascal, equivalent to a newton per square meter, and it differs from total force.
major_error_concepts: Assuming the same total force always gives the same pressure regardless of contact area.
cards.prompt: What is Pressure? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Normal force divided by area.
Distinguish pressure from force.

accepted_variants: Temperature is a state variable; heat is a transfer.
cards.definition: Temperature characterizes thermal state, while heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference. Heat transfer can change temperature or drive a phase change, so the terms are not interchangeable.
major_error_concepts: Calling an object's temperature the amount of heat it contains.
cards.prompt: What is Temperature versus Heat? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Thermal state versus energy transfer.
Heat need not always cause a temperature change.

cards.definition: A physical field assigns a quantity to each point in space and possibly time. A scalar field assigns values such as temperature, while a vector field assigns directed quantities such as gravitational acceleration.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a field exists only where a test object has been placed.
cards.prompt: What is Physical Field? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Quantity assigned throughout space or spacetime.
Scalar and vector fields differ.

accepted_variants: The source property for electric interactions.
cards.definition: Electric charge is a conserved property associated with electromagnetic interactions, occurring with positive and negative signs. Net charge is distinct from the total number of charged constituents because opposite charges can cancel.
major_error_concepts: Claiming an electrically neutral object contains no charged particles.
cards.prompt: What is Electric Charge? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Signed conserved electromagnetic property.
Net charge sums signed contributions.

cards.definition: Electric current is the rate at which net charge crosses a chosen surface, I=dQ/dt. Conventional current follows positive-charge flow, which can oppose electron drift in a metal.
major_error_concepts: Defining conventional current direction as electron drift in every material.
cards.prompt: What is Electric Current? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Charge flow per unit time.
Conventional direction distinguished from electron motion.

cards.definition: Electric potential difference is electric potential-energy change per unit charge between locations in the electrostatic setting. It is measured in volts, or joules per coulomb, and is not itself a force.
major_error_concepts: Calling voltage the amount of charge flowing per second.
cards.prompt: What is Electric Potential Difference? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Energy difference per charge.
Distinguish potential difference from force and current.

accepted_variants: Opposition to current quantified by the voltage-current relation.
cards.definition: Electrical resistance relates potential difference to current through R=V/I for a specified operating point when the ratio is meaningful. Ohmic behavior means a proportional relation with approximately constant resistance over the stated conditions.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every device obeys a constant-resistance law at all voltages.
cards.prompt: What is Electrical Resistance? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Voltage-current ratio.
Constant resistance is a model property, not universal.

cards.definition: A wave is a propagating disturbance or field pattern that can transfer energy and information. Medium elements can oscillate locally without traveling alongside the pattern, and electromagnetic waves do not require a material medium.
major_error_concepts: Assuming all waves require a material medium or move each medium particle over the full propagation distance.
cards.prompt: What is Wave? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Propagation of a disturbance.
Pattern motion differs from material transport.

cards.definition: For a linear wave model, superposition means the total disturbance equals the sum of constituent disturbances. Interference follows from adding signed amplitudes, while energy generally does not add pointwise without cross terms.
major_error_concepts: Applying exact superposition to arbitrary strongly nonlinear waves.
cards.prompt: What is Wave Superposition? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Linear sum of disturbances.
Amplitude superposition differs from naive energy addition.

cards.definition: Period T is time per cycle and frequency f is cycles per unit time, with f=1/T. Angular frequency is omega=2 pi f and uses radians per time rather than cycles per time.
major_error_concepts: Equating angular frequency and ordinary frequency numerically without the conversion factor.
cards.prompt: What is Period and Frequency? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Reciprocal period-frequency relation.
Angular frequency includes 2 pi.

cards.definition: For a periodic traveling wave, phase speed satisfies v=f lambda, where lambda is wavelength and f frequency. In dispersive systems, speed can depend on frequency and phase speed can differ from group speed.
major_error_concepts: Assuming all wave speeds are independent of frequency in every medium.
cards.prompt: What is Wave-Speed Relation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Speed equals frequency times wavelength for the periodic pattern.
Distinguish phase and group speed when needed.

accepted_variants: Movement of energy into or out of a system.
cards.definition: Energy transfer moves energy across a chosen system boundary through mechanisms such as work, heat, radiation, or transported matter. Total-energy accounting distinguishes transfer from conversion among forms inside the system.
major_error_concepts: Calling conversion from kinetic to internal energy destruction of energy.
cards.prompt: What is Energy Transfer? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Boundary transfer versus internal transformation.
Mechanism depends on the system.

accepted_variants: An equilibrium robust to sufficiently small perturbations.
cards.definition: A stable equilibrium is one for which sufficiently small perturbations remain near the equilibrium under the specified dynamics. Restoring tendencies often indicate stability, but damping and attraction are separate properties.
major_error_concepts: Equating equilibrium alone with stability or requiring every stable motion to stop.
cards.prompt: What is Stable Equilibrium? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Small disturbances remain small.
Stability need not imply return with decay.

cards.definition: A dimensionless quantity has no net physical dimensions because its constituent units cancel. It can still convey physical information, as with a ratio, angle in radians, or a dimensionless control parameter.
major_error_concepts: Assuming dimensionless quantities cannot affect a physical prediction.
cards.prompt: What is Dimensionless Quantity? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Net dimensions cancel.
Dimensionless does not mean physically meaningless.

cards.definition: A measurement is an observation-based estimate with uncertainty, while a prediction follows from a model and inputs. Comparing them requires uncertainties and matching definitions; disagreement can indicate measurement, parameter, or model limitations.
major_error_concepts: Adjusting the definition after seeing a discrepancy and calling that an independent successful prediction.
cards.prompt: What is Measurement versus Prediction? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Observation estimate versus model consequence.
Compare like quantities with uncertainty.

accepted_variants: Intermediate precision retained to avoid premature rounding.
cards.definition: Guard digits are extra digits retained during intermediate calculations to reduce accumulated rounding error. Final reporting should reflect justified precision rather than all digits retained internally.
major_error_concepts: Displaying every calculator digit as experimentally significant.
cards.prompt: What is Guard Digits? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Keep extra internal digits; round the final result appropriately.
